title: 3 Ways to Rescue a Feedback Conversation That’s Going Nowhere
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain addresses the common experience of a feedback conversation that stalls as the employee disengages and the manager's points fail to land. Drawing on his own anxiety about difficult conversations, he offers three recovery moves. First, reframe the conversation from criticism to collaborative problem-solving, illustrated by turning an accusation about late reports into a question about meeting deadlines. Second, ask open-ended questions so the exchange stops being a one-way monologue, supported by the Situation-Behavior-Impact model for structuring feedback. Third, use silence strategically to give the other person room to process, which he links to psychological safety as identified in Google's Project Aristotle. The piece closes with a preparation exercise for planning an upcoming feedback session around these three steps.
points: Stalled feedback usually feels like criticism rather than collaboration, so the first fix is to shift from what went wrong to how the problem might be solved.
Replacing a 'why' question such as 'Why did you miss the deadline?' with an open question about challenges faced invites reflection instead of defensiveness.
The SBI model (Situation-Behavior-Impact) is recommended as a structure for keeping feedback specific and concrete.
Deliberate pauses give the recipient time to process and signal patience, contributing to the psychological safety that Project Aristotle ties to team effectiveness.
quotes: These conversations have a typical path: you start with good intentions, but somewhere along the way, the conversation stalls. The employee checks out, the points you want to make aren’t landing, and you’re left wondering, “What went wrong?

I’ve been there more times than I can count. I still remember sweating over the prospect of having a difficult conversation with a team member, even when I had all the information and data to back up my feedback.

When a feedback conversation stalls, it’s often because the message feels like criticism rather than collaboration. The first step in turning things around is to reframe the conversation. Instead of focusing on what went wrong, shift the focus to problem-solving.

Another reason feedback conversations go nowhere is because they feel like a one-way street. If you’re the only one talking, it’s time to pass the mic. Ask open-ended questions that encourage reflection and an open conversation.

When the conversation hits a wall, silence can be your friend. Pausing allows the other person time to process what has been said and think about their response. It also shows that you are patient, and respectful, of the time they need to process the feedback.

This tactic also helps create an environment of psychological safety, where the other person feels they have the space to reflect without pressure. According to Google’s Project Aristotle, psychological safety is one of the top factors in team effectiveness.
